text: Most machine-learning algorithms do arithmetic, so they need numbers. But real tables are full of text categories — city, plan type, payment method. Encoding converts those categories into numbers, and how you do it matters. The wrong encoding quietly tells the model something false, like Chicago is twice Boston.

Nominal categories have no natural order — city, color, payment method. Ordinal categories have a meaningful order — plan level, education level, survey ratings. The choice of encoding follows directly from this split. With 300 illustrative customers, spend depends on city, and we'll exploit that to show the mistake.

One-hot encoding replaces a column with one 0 or 1 column per category — a row gets a 1 in its own category's column and 0 everywhere else, implying no order at all. handle_unknown equals ignore matters in real life — new data will eventually contain a city never seen in training, and this setting turns it into all zeros instead of raising an error.

This is a learned transformation — the encoder remembers the categories it saw during fit — so, following last lesson's rule, fit on the training set only, then transform validation and test. pandas's get_dummies does the same job but doesn't remember categories, which is risky for train-test consistency.

When the order is real, map categories to integers in that order explicitly — basic to 0, standard to 1, premium to 2. You must state the order yourself; otherwise the encoder defaults to alphabetical, which would put premium before basic entirely wrong.

What happens if you number a nominal column anyway? Fitting two linear regressions predicting spend from city — one with Atlanta, Boston, Chicago numbered 0, 1, 2, and one with proper one-hot columns. The fake-ordering model explains only 4 percent of the variation in spend.

Because it can only draw a straight line through 0, 1, 2, Boston, which sits in the middle alphabetically but has the highest spend, can never be predicted higher than both its neighbors. One-hot encoding, letting each city have its own level, explains 81.5 percent of the variation instead — a massive difference for the exact same underlying data.

Tree-based models are less sensitive to this particular mistake, since they split on thresholds rather than drawing straight lines, but a linear or distance-based model will be badly misled. One-hot is the safe default for nominal data. For columns with thousands of distinct values, like zip codes, group rare categories into other, use frequency encoding, or carefully use target encoding — though that's a classic leakage trap unless computed only inside the training data.

To recap: use one-hot for nominal categories and explicit-order ordinal encoding for ordered ones. Never number unordered categories for a linear or distance-based model. Set handle_unknown to ignore, fit encoders on training data only, and plan ahead for high-cardinality columns. Next up, lesson 10: scaling and normalization.
